articles.title: Under 30, latinos e donne, chi ha voltato le spalle al tycoon
articles.summary: Caro vita e guerra all'Iran spingono la 'blue wave', si sgretola la coalizione Maga
articles.preview: Under 30, latinos, ceto medio e donne, ma anche gli afroamericani tornati alle urne e una parte dell'elettorato maschile che nel 2024 aveva voltato le spalle ai Dem: la mappa dello tsunami azzurro che ha consegnato al partito dell'asinello le chiavi di Capitol Hill è la fotografia quasi speculare della coalizione che due anni fa alimentò la 'valanga rossa' della seconda vittoria di Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Under 30, latinos, ceto medio e donne, ma anche gli afroamericani tornati alle urne e una parte dell'elettorato maschile che nel 2024 aveva voltato le spalle ai Dem: la mappa dello tsunami azzurro che ha consegnato al partito dell'asinello le chiavi di Capitol Hill è la fotografia quasi speculare della coalizione che due anni fa alimentò la 'valanga rossa' della seconda vittoria di Donald Trump.

Caro-vita, ma anche la guerra all'Iran e la corruzione hanno spinto l'ondata blu che ha fatto crollare la diga della coalizione Maga in territori tradizionalmente conservatori, dal Texas al Kansas, provocando un radicale ripensamento tra gli elettori che per due volte avevano portato Trump a vincere la Casa Bianca. L'affluenza di metà mandato è generalmente inferiore a quella delle presidenziali (non stavolta però con oltre 61 milioni ancor prima del 3 novembre) e il voto tende quasi sempre a penalizzare il partito del presidente, ma i risultati quest'anno hanno segnato traguardi storici per i Dem che hanno vinto per la prima volta dopo decenni in vari Stati con un vantaggio su scala nazionale del 13% nel voto per la Camera, un record dal 1976.

Aree rurali, sobborghi e grandi città si sono spostati in 'zona blu' con vantaggi a due cifre. Analizzando i gruppi demografici, nel 2024 il voto della Gen Z che si abbevera su podcast e social era stato determinante per Trump e i Maga mentre stavolta, secondo gli exit polls dell'Ap, sette Under 30 su dieci hanno votato Dem. Altro tassello fondamentale sono stati gli ispanici, sia pure con differenze tra Florida, Texas, New York o California.

Trump aveva costruito parte del successo del 2024 sui latinos, soprattutto uomini e classe lavoratrice. Due anni dopo sei ispanici su dieci hanno scelto i Dem, mentre solo un terzo ha sostenuto i repubblicani. Tra i test più clamorosi, uno arriva dalla Rio Grande Valley, nel Texas meridionale dove i Dem si sono imposti con vantaggi a due cifre in tre collegi della Camera che Trump aveva stravinto due anni fa, e questo nonostante il ridisegno dei collegi elettorali, il cosiddetto gerrymandering, voluto dal Gop nel biennio prima del voto per blindare le possibilità di vittoria. Anche gli afroamericani, che in precedenti cicli elettorali nel dopo Barack Obama erano rimasti a casa, hanno rappresentato una componente importante del successo Dem votando in massa in stati come Georgia, Florida, Texas e Michigan.

Le donne, tradizionalmente Dem, hanno confermato il loro sostegno: tra le elettrici sotto i trent'anni la percentuale ha raggiunto il 75%. Ma soprattutto il voto è stato un referendum contro Trump e contro i suoi candidati, due dei quali - Ken Paxton in Texas e Darline Graham in South Carolina - sono stati umiliati dal risultato delle urne. A dispetto delle promesse della Casa Bianca, tre elettori su quattro hanno bocciato l'economia: tra questi il 67% ha votato Dem, contro il 29% che ha sostenuto i repubblicani, mentre quasi l'80% degli intervistati degli exit polls Ap ha dichiarato che l'inflazione ha messo in difficoltà la propria famiglia.

E' stato così che, motivati dalla rabbia per il prezzo del macinato e della benzina, gli americani hanno voltato le spalle a Trump con conseguenze così devastanti che - ha pronosticato su X il governatore uscente della Florida Ron DeSantis - il partito dell'elefante "dovrà aspettare almeno il 2032 per avere una chance di tornare a controllare il Senato".

articles.title: Presidential hopeful Vance appears to question Iran war after polls debacle
articles.summary: Vance cited trusted pollster saying Iran war, Israel ties were top of mind for Trump voters swinging to Democrats.
articles.preview: Vance cites trusted pollster saying Iran war and Israel ties were top of mind for Trump voters swinging to Democrats. US Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the United States Congress to Democrats. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X.
articles.body:
Vance cites trusted pollster saying Iran war and Israel ties were top of mind for Trump voters swinging to Democrats.

US Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the United States Congress to Democrats.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Mark Pfeifle, who served as deputy national security adviser under President George W Bush, told Al Jazeera that Vance was owning up to a political failure of the administration’s own making.

“If you mess up, fess up!” he said, saying Vance was speaking up to convey that “my name was on the ballot two years ago. I have to take responsibility for this”, in a sign of political maturity and readiness to tackle Republicans’ biggest political liabilities.

MAGA heir

Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to US President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, has been a key negotiator as the US and Iran search for a way out of the eight-month conflict, which has dented their economies and pushed global fuel prices up.

His statements on Tehran have been more dovish than those of other key members of the administration, and his post-election note appears to mark the closest he has yet come to publicly diverging from Trump on an issue that looks set to dog Republicans as the war continues.

“Vance is definitely trying to distance himself from Trump, as many other respectable Republicans will do over the next several weeks and months,” said Nick Rahall, a former Democratic member of Congress. “The people have spoken.”

“It had even leaked before that JD was the only one in Trump’s inner circle who had questions and was hesitant about Iran [war] from the beginning,” Rahall added.

Citing a pollster he describes as “one of the smartest people I know”, Vance said he was told ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given by Americans surveyed who had voted for Trump in 2024 but were planning to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms.

In stark contrast, Trump said, in the wake of the rebuke at the ballot box, that he had no regrets about launching the conflict.

“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal.

articles.title: UK politics: Burnham says US midterm results have created ‘opportunity’ for world to focus on cost of living and ending Iran war – as it happened
articles.summary: ‘I think people want to see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people,’ PM says Louise Haigh starts by saying she is standing in for Andy Burnham. articles.body:
Burnham says US election results have created 'opportunity' for world to focus on cutting cost of living and ending Iran war

Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures.

In an interview at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, asked if he was worried the results might make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham replied:

President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.

That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves.

But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. The conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.

These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that. And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do.

Some politicians and commentators have interpreted the results as evidence that rightwing populism is in retreat around the world. But when asked if he thought the elections were part of a global pattern, Burnham was reluctant to make that claim. Instead, he replied:

I think people want to see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people, and that’s what the voters, in my view, are saying in the United States.

Let’s get focused in a laser-like way on those cost of living issues. And I think around the world there’s a recognition that countries can’t do that on their own, and can’t do that when we have division between nations.

I’ve been working hard as prime minister to bring a new approach, a new approach in the Middle East, and the foreign secretary set that out [with the announcements about sanctions on illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank].

A new approach to Europe, and we believe that will help us get growth back up and reduce those cost of living pressures. But a new approach with the Commonwealth too.

Asked if Britain would be pushing for de-escalation in the Iran war, Burnham said:

I’ll be working for de-escalation. To make it very clear, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again. That’s what we will be working towards.

Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures. (See 1.53pm.)

The government has said that the visitor levy bill, legislation giving powers to local leaders to impose a levy on visitors staying overnight that was introduced in the Commons today, is “the most significant step in making fiscal devolution a reality”.

The government has also introduced into parliament the energy independence bill, which it says is “a down payment on longer-term reforms that will fix Britain’s broken energy system, putting affordability at its heart, while unlocking barriers to deliver clean power”.

How accurate were Haigh and Burghart's facts at PMQs?

The Press Association’s QuickCheck service has been looking at some of the facts cited by Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, and Alex Burghart, the deputy Tory leader, at PMQs. Here are three figures that it suggests are potentially misleading.

Burghart claimed the OBR report said 215,000 jobs were at risk from the government’s tax rises.

PA says he seemed to be quoting a figure that applied to the impact of the tax threshold freezes that started when the Tories were in office.

The OBR said: “Following our standard approach, we have estimated that, taken together, the threshold freezes in income tax and NICs from 2022/23 to 2030/31 could decrease labour supply by 215,000 in average-hours equivalent (AHE) terms by 2030/31.”

£183bn spent on working-age welfare?

Burghart asked Haigh how much the government was spending on working-age welfare and, when she refused to answer, he said the figure was £183bn.

PA says he seemed to be referencing a figure that covered spending for children and pensioners. It says:

The OBR forecasted total welfare spending to reach £352.7bn in the current fiscal year.

This figure falls to about £182.8bn when excluding certain spending on pensioners. This might be the figure Mr Burghart was referencing, however it includes £13.7bn of child benefit spending.

This figure also includes attendance allowance, which is a disability benefit paid to those of state pension age.

Separate data show the Department for Work and Pensions spending on benefits for working-age people is set to reach £136.1bn in 2026/27. This does not include welfare spending from other departments, such as HM Revenue and Customs.

Welfare spending rising £88bn under the Tories?

Haigh said welfare spending rose by £88bn in a decade under the Tories.

PA says this is close to what OBR and DWP figures say. But those are cash figures, it says. “In real terms, a measure which offsets for inflation, the DWP figure rose by a more modest £21.8bn,” PA says.

UNHCR criticises UK’s 30-year ‘earned settlement’ plans for refugees

The UN refugee agency has said a government plan to make refugees wait up to 30 years before they get permission to settle in the UK “raises significant concerns”. Diane Taylor has the story.

Legislation aimed at ensuring more major sporting events are held in the UK is poised to become law after being approved by MPs this afternoon. As the Press Association reports, the sporting events bill is modelled on bespoke laws passed for the London 2012 Olympic and Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games and creates a framework for future events. It will support competitions such as the upcoming Uefa European football championship in 2028, in addition to future bids, such as the UK’s application to host the Fifa Women’s World Cup in 2035.

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, told MPs the bill would allow the government “to stand ready to host the biggest events in the world”, and added the UK had already bid to host the 2029 World Para Athletics Championships.

The bill has already gone through the House of Lords.

Andy Burnham tried his hand at playing the steel drum during his trip to the Caribbean, the Press Association reports. PA says:

The PM played Mary Had A Little Lamb while in Antigua for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting. After his performance of the nursery rhyme, he was told by director Khan Cordice of the Hell’s Gate steel orchestra “you’re a musician”, to which Burnham modestly replied: “I play a little music.”

He was later joined by foreign secretary Ed Miliband for a duet of the nursery rhyme.

Burnham has previously shown off his musical skills on the guitar, including playing a song by The Smiths after being handed an instrument by a Ukrainian soldier on a visit to Kyiv.

Swinney rejects call for review of law saying people with limited rights to live in UK can stand as MSPs

Severin Carrell

Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.

John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, has rejected calls from MSPs for a review of laws which allow people with limited rights to live in the UK to stand for Holyrood.

Yesterday the standards, procedures and public appointments committee, chaired by the Scottish National party MSP Jenni Minto, said the reforms could undermine “fragile” confidence amongst voters in the country’s institutions.

Swinney told LBC he had no plans to review the provisions, which first came into force this year in the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025. He said:

We don’t intend to do so, no. The parliament voted unanimously for the provision for foreign nationals to be able to stand for elections in certain circumstances.

The reforms came under intense scrutiny after the May election after the Conservatives and Reform UK protested about the election of Q Manivannan, an Indian citizen, for the Scottish Greens in Edinburgh and Lothians East region.

A post-graduate student at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, given them right to remain until the end of 2029.

Swinney’s government is bidding to expand the provisions of the act by including Commonwealth citizens, who were excluded as a category last year. Swinney told LBC “the government will press ahead with that.” Manivannan only qualified because they were on a student visa, not because they were a Commonwealth citizen.

The act covers elections to Holyrood and Scottish councils; Westminster contests in Scotland are reserved to Westminster and excluded.

The Department for Work and Pensions’ report released today on the employment of disabled people (see 2.41pm) says that the financial year ending 2026 was the first for more than a decade where the number of disabled working-age people in the UK fell. It says it is too early to know if this was just temporary. It explains:

This (FYE [financial year ending] 2026) is the first full year since financial year ending (FYE) 2014 where the number of disabled people and disability prevalence have decreased, by 0.5% (around 50,000) and by 0.2 percentage points, respectively. It is too early to determine whether this is a temporary change, also as the latest quarterly data for April to June 2026 reports a year-on-year significant increase in the number of disabled people (250,000).

OBR tells MPs it is not in position to confirm Tory claim ILR U-turn will cost £10bn

The Commons Treasury committee has started taking evidence from officials from the Office for Budget Responsibility about the budget. Harriett Baldwin, a Conservative member of the committee, asked about Shabana Mahmood’s announcement on Monday axing some of the restrictions to indefinite leave to remain (ILR) that had been planned by the Home Office.

The Tories claim this U-turn will cost the exchequer £10bn.

Asked what impact this announcement would have on the OBR’s fiscal assumptions, Tom Josephs, a member of the OBR’s budget responsibility committee, said the OBR would have to review this for its next forecast in the spring. He said he could not give an answer now.

Asked if he thought it really would cost £10bn, Josephs said “that is not an estimate that we produced”. He said that was a government estimate for the lifetime cost of some migrants.

Asked if the change on Monday would be "material enough” to require a change to the OBR’s forecast, Josephs just said the OBR would assess the policy as a whole. “If we think [the Monday announcement is] significant enough to adjust the forecast, then we will do so.”

Mahmood originally produced the £10bn figure to justify the plans she originally announced last year. She said making it harder for migrant workers to get ILR would save the government £10bn over time.

This claim backfired when Mahmood U-turned on a large part of her plan, leading the Tories to claim she was now in effect raising spending by almost £10bn (because the savings were forgone).

Almost half of Neet young people classed as disabled, DWP figures show

Just under half of young people not in work, education or training were classed as disabled in the year to March – a proportion which has more than doubled in just over a decade, the Press Association reports. PA says:

The government is currently working on reducing the number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training – known as Neets – with a review expected to be published in the coming weeks making recommendations for changes in the system.

The number of Neets topped a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade, fuelling calls for more help to get young people into work.

Government data published today showed 45.3% of Neets were classed as disabled in the year to March.

The Department for Work and Pensions said this was a rise of 24.2 percentage points since the proportion of 21.1% in the 12 months to March 2014.

The latest data showed disabled young people were more than three times as likely to be Neet compared to non-disabled young people – 30.2% compared with 8.6%.

Depression, bad nerves or anxiety was the most common main health condition reported by disabled Neets, accounting for almost a quarter (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%).

Burnham claims there's 'solution' to Poundland's problems, as he urges its bosses to work with government on rescue plan

Andy Burnham has urged Poundland bosses to work with the government on trying to find a “practical solution” to the problems that have left the company on the brink of administration.

In a pooled interview, asked if he had a message for Poundland executives, Burnham replied:

Focus on the people in your employment, meet with the business secretary because we are setting up that meeting, come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions, they’re on high streets, they matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let’s find it.

When it was put to him that there was a limit to what the government could do if the company was not profitable, he replied:

There’s always a limit, but we’re prepared to find what we can do. We believe in this instance there is a solution. There are many viable outlets here. Other retailers are expressing interest. Get around the table. Let’s find a solution.

While the public here in the UK - which overwhelmingly believes his presidency has been bad for Britain - may welcome the ‘blue tsunami’, ministers and officials will be watching nervously for how Trump reacts.

The US president acknowledged overnight the Iran conflict - which has pushed up the cost of living globally - had cost the Republicans votes and has previously suggested a deal could be struck with Tehran post-midterms.

But there are concerns here that a bruised Trump - whose domestic agenda is constrained after losing control of Congress but who still wields a veto and significant power over foreign policy - could now lash out like a caged animal.

There could be a backlash on the world stage as he tries to cement his legacy during his last two years, potentially including more military action in Iran, Ukraine and even Cuba; more trade tariffs; and more unhelpful interventions in UK and European politics.

But for now, there is also relief that the US has cast its verdict on Trump and his combative style of politics, and hope that if the Democrats get their act together (for this was a referendum on the US president rather than a ringing endorsement of his opponents), the 2028 election could transform the special relationship.

If you are deputising at PMQs, it may be nice to get a good write-up from the sketchwriters, and satisfying to craft a line that will play well on the TV or radio later, but, frankly, one task matters above all others: don’t mess up. And, in that respect, Louise Haigh and Alex Burghart both performed well – in exchanges likely to be quickly forgotten.

For Haigh, this was her first time, but it did not particularly sound like this. She sounded confident and authoritative, without being brash and hubristic. She did not have anything very new to say about welfare, and Labour does not have a firm answer yet to the question as to when it will cut the benefits bill, but Haigh swerved this quite adequately with attacks on the Tories’ record and by making the Labour argument about now wanting welfare spending on failure. She said:

We have been repeatedly clear that we cannot afford to pay for failure and must invest in success – and that is how we will bring the welfare bill down.

We will make support more conditional on taking up opportunities, ensuring young people get help they need earlier, tackling the long-term drivers of welfare spending, including high housing costs, and we will do all this in a Labour way.

She would not rule out tax rises to pay for more welfare spending (see 2.16pm), but that was the sort of question opposition parties ask when they can’t think of a proper, specific one and so instead have to resort to simplistic politics-by-slogan.

Burghart has done PMQs before, and he was a bit more polished. His pre-scripted riffs about “two 10-year plans in 10 months”, and John Healey’s Today programme welfare gaffe last week, were elegantly done, but not quite withering or funny enough to be truly damaging. He didn’t fail, but he didn’t score.

The most interesting question came from the Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper, who is probably the first MP to get a ‘Trump might be a rapist’ allegation into Hansard. (See 12.29pm.) Rather ingeniously, she tried to suggest there might be some sort of UK government angle. But there probably isn’t. This is one for Congress.

If anyone had a bad PMQs, it was probably Lindsay Hoyle. It was not clear who he was referring to when he delivered his ‘don’t shout a woman down’ bollocking to some Tory MP. (See 12.20pm.) But it sounded a bit chauvinist. Haigh is the second most senior person in government; she seemed perfectly capable of coping with a bit of heckling; and if shouting down a minister is unacceptable, it should not matter what sex they are.

Munira Wilson (Lib Dem) says Haigh recently said the government would give local leaders more power to invest in things that matter. But it is cutting funding for Richmond council by more than £100m over the next four years, 60% of its budget? Will Haigh meet her to discuss this to find a solution.

Haigh says the government inherited an unfair council funding system. She offers Wilson a meeting with a minister.

Bobby Dean (Lib Dem) asks if the government will back legislation to make US tech companies pay fair compensation to victims of online scams. He says, given the US election results, the government should be tougher with the US administration.

Haigh says the Online Safety Act requires tech companies to take robust action on online scams.

"We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X. articles.body:
Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections.

"We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X.

"If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.

Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.

In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".

He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."

Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".

In recent weeks, Trump has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - who has not been seen in public since he was reportedly seriously wounded in the same Israeli air strike on the first day of the war that killed his father and predecessor, Ali - said he did not expect US policy to change.

Khamenei released a statement saying anyone who thought there would be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" was "gravely mistaken".

He also said the war would have "much wider dimensions" if it resumed.

In a separate development on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been intercepted, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.

BBC Verify has been investigating the IRGC claims, and has not found any evidence that four tankers were destroyed.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said a tanker was struck by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles (26km) north-east of Limah, in Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening. No casualties were reported, it added.

On Monday, an Indian crew member of a dhow - a wooden sailing boat - was killed in an attack north-east of Limah. Thirteen other crew members were rescued by Omani authorities.

The IRCG also reported on Wednesday that its forces had shot down another US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.

It made a similar claim on Monday night, when US officials said the US military had carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

- US midterms: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

- Published14 hours ago

In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterms, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he did not consider them to be "really in a war".

When asked about what the newspaper described as "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".

Indirect talks to end the conflict have been stalled for months.

President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained on Tuesday that his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue".

"No-one will benefit from this war" if it were to resume, he warned.

He also emphasised that Iran's supreme leader had granted the government powers to negotiate "issues that he had previously considered off-limits".

Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqai said on Monday that the basis of the current indirect negotiations mediated by Qatar remained a seven-step proposal that Iran submitted in September. But he added that the proposal had been "condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days".

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking at a press conference following a meeting with Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar in Cairo, el-Sissi cautioned that further escalation could trigger additional crises, with repercussions extending beyond the region to the wider world.

El-Sissi urged both sides to pursue a political solution through dialogue.

He also reiterated Egypt's rejection to any threats against Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations, reaffirming his country’s position that their security is an integral part of Arab national security.

"I reaffirm Egypt's categorical rejection of any threat that may affect the security and stability of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the other brotherly Gulf states. 40 killed, more than 30 missing after 'insane' Russian attack on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – fresh back from his meetings in Germany yesterday and today – has offered an update on the search and rescue operations after the Russian strike on a school in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.

40 people have been confirmed dead, with fears that more than 30 may still be under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.

“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that 40 people were confirmed dead and more than 30 missing after “insane” Russian attack on a school in Ukraine on Monday (14:44), just days before key trilateral peace talks with the US and Russia.

Zelenskyy continues his trip of Europe and after visiting Germany where he was hosted by chancellor Friedrich Merz, he is now expected in Spain.

His comments came as the EU hosted key technical talks with the US, some EU countries, Nato, and the World Bank on Ukraine (10:05).

Following the US midterm elections, some European leaders expressed hopes that the result will put Donald Trump under pressure to make progress in talks with Moscow and Kyiv (12:18, 12:57, 14:31).

But some leaders also expressed concerns about the political consequences of the vote (11:31, 11:55, 12:45).

In other news,

Montenegro could be in a position to join the European Union as early as 2028 with accession negotiations concluded by the end of this year, after the bloc praised the country for advancing “the reforms needed” to complete the process (13:33).

If you are after more reactions to the US midterm elections, you can follow our US live blog here:

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy lands in Spain for talks with key Ibero-American leaders

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has landed in Spain, where he is expected to take part in talks with key leaders from Spain and Latin America, as well as the UN secretary-general and the European Council president, according to Spain’s El País newspaper.

The paper reported that Zelenskyy will take part in “several high-level meetings” on the sidelines of the Ibero-American summit in Madrid, hosted by Spain’s embattled prime minister Pedro Sánchez.

Argetina’s controversial president Javier Milei is believed to be among the guests. Portugal will be represented by PM Luís Montenegro.

Just like in Berlin, Zelenskyy’s trip was kept secret until his plane touched down for security reasons, El País said.

French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe

Jon Henley

Europe correspondent

In other news, France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.

The French blood service (EFS) saidtemperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.

The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.

Here is some more on how Italy’s far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who once had good relations with Donald Trump, dismissed questions about the midterm election results, telling journalists “let’s talk about America another time”.

Meloni, wearing a red suit, had been door-stepped while attending a ceremony in central Rome on Wednesday to mark Italy’s national unity and armed forces day and didn’t welcome the journalistic focus on the US midterms.

“I see you’re very interested in the celebration of the republic and the Armed Forces,” she said sarcastically.

Meloni had positioned herself as a key European ally to Trump until April, when the pair fell out, firstly over Italy’s refusal to support the US-Israeli war in Italy and then because of Trump’s extraordinary broadside against Pope Leo in reaction to the pontiff’s condemnation of the war.

They had appeared to be getting relations back on track at the G7 summit in June before Trump claimed Meloni had begged him to take a photo with him - a story Meloni said was a “a total invention”.

Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani did instead comment on the midterms, saying Italy’s relationship with the US “remains unchanged regardless of who is in government or the parliamentary situation”.

In an interview with the Rome-based newspaper, Il Messaggero, Tajani said “we have never been Trumpians” and “Meloni isn’t a Maga supporter either – heaven forbid!”

The League, which is led by joint deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini, who until fairly recently continuously praised Trump, said in a statement:

“When a population votes, their vote must always be respected and understood.”

The party also expressed hope that the outcome would speed-up efforts to end wars and restore peace.

European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that “US voters have made their choice clear”, commenting on the country’s midterms election results.

She said she hoped Congress would continue to support Ukraine and put more pressure on Russia.

“I hope that the new Congress... will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia,” Kallas said, adding that Europe and the United States “are much stronger together” in pushing Moscow to end its war.

The European Union has offered fresh hope for Serbia’s membership talks if the election-winning student movement there forms a government willing to strengthen democracy.

The election of a diverse student-led opposition movement could provide an opening for a reset with the most influential of the western Balkan countries in line at Europe’s door, AP reported.

“Now Serbia has the chance for a fresh start,” enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told EU lawmakers as she debriefed them on the report.

“The new Serbian government has an opportunity to turn the page, strengthen democratic institutions and fundamental rights and take the necessary steps to advance on Serbia’s accession path,” she added.

Serbia could progress rapidly under a government with strong political will but membership currently looks years away.

It comes as the the European Commission said in its enlargement report that Montenegro is on track to become the EU’s 28th member in 2028 (see post 12.33) - and that Albania and Moldova could join the following year.

However, Ukraine is unlikely to meet the conditions for joining before the end of the decade.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – fresh back from his meetings in Germany yesterday and today – has offered an update on the search and rescue operations after the Russian strike on a school in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.

40 people have been confirmed dead, with fears that more than 30 may still be under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.

“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”

Germany's Wadephul sees both 'continuity and change' after US midterms, hopes for breakthrough on Ukraine

German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has said the results of the US midterm elections will mean some “continuity” in Germany’s relations with the Trump administration, but also a “change” in ties with the US Democrats as he hoped to see some breakthrough on Ukraine.

Berlin will “continue to seek common ground” with the Trump administration, “striving for compromise” on key issues in the face of global challenges.

But these elections “also signal change” as the Democratic Party’s success – which he noted was “of a magnitude rare in American history” – will “likely seek to shift the political discourse in the US.”

He said he did not “any complications” arising from this result, and noted that the political engagement will now need to be “broader” and “perhaps even more interesting in certain aspects.”

He said many foreign policy issues featured prominently in the US elections, including tariffs and the war in Iran.

Wadephul added that he hoped for “more dialogue in Congress, across party lines, about what can be done collectively to support Ukraine.

“I think they’ve been holding back on that issue for quite some time now during the election campaign,” he said.

“I also know that in both chambers – and within both parties – there are staunch supporters of Ukraine who clearly recognise that this Russian war of aggression threatens not only security and freedom in Europe but also in the United States.”

Montenegro could sign EU accession treaty in mid 2027, European Commission says

The European Union could conclude accession negotiations with Montenegro by the end of this year and could sign an accession treaty with the country as soon as June 2027, the European Commission said, as reported by Reuters.

“For the first time since 2011, when the EU closed accession negotiations with Croatia, the EU is in a position to soon close accession negotiations with another candidate country, Montenegro,” the EU’s executive said in its annual enlargement policy report.

“This is testament to Montenegro’s sustained efforts to advance on the European path and implement the reforms needed to turn EU membership into reality,” it said, adding that “it considers that accession negotiations could realistically be closed by the end of 2026”.

If the accession treaty gets signed in mid-2027, Montenegro could join the bloc as early as 2028, German news agency dpa says.

Joining the bloc requires all current 27 member countries to ratify an accession treaty.

Kremlin says it hopes midterm results do not affect Trump's 'peacemaking efforts'

Meanwhile, the Kremlin said that it hopes that the results of the US midterm elections will not impact what it said were president Donald Trump’s “peacemaking efforts" on Ukraine, Reuters said.

In comments broadcast by Russian state media, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said:

“We are sincerely counting on [Trump] continuing his peacemaking efforts.“

'Governing in the US will be almost impossible,' Belgian defence ministers worries

Belgian defence minister Theo Francken has warned that “governing in the US will be almost impossible in the coming years,” but said that Europe’s priorities should be on trade, Ukraine and Nato.

Writing on X, he said in a post translated by Reuters:

“Governing in the United States will be almost impossible in the coming years given the level of internal division and polarisation. As a European politician I will mainly look of course to trade policies, support to Ukraine and Nato.”

'Democracy won in America,' Tusk declares alongside Czech Republic's Babiš

Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš is in Warsaw today, meeting with Poland’s Donald Tusk, and unsurprisingly both leaders were asked for their thoughts on the US elections.

Babiš briefly chuckled in response to the question, before saying the results were “as expected,” but stressed the significance of the Republican party losing in places like Texas, where they “ruled for decades.”

He said that Trump will still have “major competence,” and he hoped that the US president would use them to focus on the issues that he promised he’d resolve: ending the Russian invasion on Ukraine and the crisis in the Hormuz strait.

“I am not expecting some sort of major change … but let’s see what he comes up with. What we need … is to end these two wars,” he said, stressing their costs for Europe.

Poland’s Tusk declares: “Today, democracy won in America.”

“Democracy is amazing; I love democracy, it’s a beautiful thing,” he said, absolutely beaming.

He then added:

“I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region, but then Trump is still the president. … My advice would be not to overuse the veto … as a sort of method of governing,” an apparent domestic swipe at Poland’s opposition president and Trump ally, Karol Nawrocki, with whom he is locked in a bitter dispute over the country’s constitutional court.

'Either he decides to rise above fray and tone down involvement, or he doesn't,' French finance minister says

French finance minister Roland Lescure also responded to the result in the US, discussing what the next steps of the US president, Donald Trump, could be.

Here are his comments, via Reuters:

“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement; or he does not.“

Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days.“

Germany's Pistorius congratulates Democrats on 'historic victory' in US midterms

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has congratulated the US Democeats “from the bottom of his heart” on their win last night, Dlf reported.

Deutsche Welle’s chief political correspondent Nina-Haase-Trobridge posted a longer clip of his comments at the Berlin Security Conference, with Pistorius acknowledging a “historic victory” for the Democrats.

“So for us this means we will continue our relationship based on trust and cooperation with the administration. … And, like in the past, we will have a close working relationship with the Democrats,” he said, quoted by the journalist.

“As for what we can expect now, that remains to be seen. It depends, to some extent, on what the American president intends to do following these elections,” he said in response to a question from Politico’s Rixa Fürsen.

'A powerful political signal about a change of course,' Norway's Støre says

Meanwhile, Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Støre told Reuters:

“This is a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.

Voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy.“

'We'll talk about America some other time,' Meloni tells reporters

Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, who also clashed with Trump in recent months, wasn’t in the mood to offer any reaction to the US elections this morning, as she told reporters, via Corriere:

“We’ll talk about America some other time. Right now, it’s Armed Forces Day, 4 November.”

But opposition politicians celebrated the result, with former prime minister Matteo Renzi calling it “wonderful” and a response to Trump’s “abuse” of his position.

“Trump has another two years to go, but the Maga movement has been severely weakened, if not defeated.”

MEP Sandro Gozi said the electorate’s verdict “offers renewed hope that the next two years will mark the beginning of the end of the Trump era.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski ridiculed the Polish right, which has been supportive of Trump since his return to the office.

Paraphrasing Jesus’s words from the Bible (sic!), he said:

“Truly I tell you, before the rooster crows, they will disown him three times”

He also took swipe at US billionaire Elon Musk who donated hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, reposting his comment from one of their previous clashes, saying:

“See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”

For what it’s worth, Musk also appeared to see a funny side in his involvement in the campaign, saying:

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

Spain's Sánchez hails progressive fightback in the US 'against hate,' draws parallels with Spain

Sam Jones

in Madrid

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results in the US, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.

“Yesterday, American society voted against the policies that only impoverish,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”

Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added:

“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”

Morning opening: EU to lead talks on support for Ukraine with US, Nato, partners

Jakub Krupa

With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leading on discussions about the next round of support for Ukraine.

The European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank, looking what can be done to help Kyiv throughout the winter and how to support the US-led peace process with the upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff said US negotiators would meet with their European partners in Brussels.

Their talks come after another night of heavy attacks on Ukraine, hitting power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr and a cargo vessel at sea near Odesa.

I will also bring you any European reactions to the midterms in the US, although many politicians (while quietly amused or relieved) may choose to stay silent to not risk Donald Trump’s wrath.

Let’s see what the day brings.

It’s Wednesday, 4 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.body:
Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.

The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog.

“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”

On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.

Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.

Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.

Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company launched Muse Code, its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook, the viral agent platform that made headlines.

AT&T’s Connected Life system now supports Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events and more.

With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home.

These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home.

AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

articles.title: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.summary: Apple's AI-powered Siri Recaps won me over in just one day, despite my privacy reservations. But there's still room for improvement.
articles.preview: On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.

After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.

The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.

It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.

Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.

Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening.

I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.

I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.

But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.

I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.

For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.

One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.

I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.

Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.

This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.

While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.

I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.

I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.

Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.

These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.

Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

articles.title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.summary: The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers.
articles.preview: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies. "No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said. Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
articles.body:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.

"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.

Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.

Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.

But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.

While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.

Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.

Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.

In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.

By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.

According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.

"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.

The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.

Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.

It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.

Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.

"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.

"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."

'Hybrid warfare' claim

A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.

In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.

But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.

"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.

According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.

Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.

"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.

"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."

Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.

Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.

But no formal attribution has been made.

None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.

But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.

Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

articles.body:
The federal government is “sleepwalking its way into another robodebt” scandal amid a lack of transparency and legislation around use of algorithms and artificial intelligence in decisions, the chief executive of independent thinktank the Centre for Public Integrity said.

Dr Catherine Williams launched the centre’s “Computer Says No” report on Thursday, which examines the use of automated decision-making (ADM) tools by the government and calls for urgent reform.

The centre is concerned Australians may not know whether ADM has been used in decisions affecting them.

Among eight recommendations, the report calls for a mandatory audit and public register of all ADM use, and an independent oversight body with powers to monitor, audit and investigate the government over it.

Williams said the report was developed amid the centre’s increasing concern about the use of an algorithm as part of the government’s integrated assessment tool (IAT), which is used to assess the level of home support older Australians are entitled to.

The IAT has been found to be routinely under-assessing people’s needs and package entitlements, with aged care assessors banned by the government from overriding incorrect algorithmic decisions.

“We have been watching the evidence emerge in relation to the aged care algorithm tool, and becoming increasingly concerned about what is clearly the lack of an appropriate and robust framework to govern use of ADM by the government,” Williams said.

“It feels as though we are sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario, and that’s why we’ve decided to put this work forward now, in the hope also that it can help inform any framework that the government does propose in relation to ADM.”

The attorney general’s department has been developing an ADM framework, with public consultation ending in January 2025.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, did not respond to questions about when a draft framework might be complete and made public but said the government “is committed to ensuring the safe and responsible use of ADM to deliver timely and efficient services for the Australian community”.

The framework will implement recommendations from the royal commission into robodebt, she said.

A report from the commonwealth ombudsman, published in October, found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission had been ignored by the government in developing and rolling out the IAT.

Rowland did not respond to questions about whether any ADM framework would be retrospective but said it “will be designed to improve accuracy and consistency of administrative decisions, embed robust safeguards, including transparency obligations, and ensure that ADM is used lawfully, responsibly, and with appropriate human oversight”.

The framework will also lift productivity and help deliver faster, more reliable services, she said.

In September, Kate Chaney, an independent MP, introduced a private member’s bill to establish the first legislated, mandatory framework for ADM use by the government.

She said the attorney general department’s consultation process for an ADM framework “finished almost two years ago”.

“I have met with the attorney general about it and they say ‘We’re working on it’. I think it’s really important that we keep the pressure up so that it doesn’t get dropped because it’s too hard.”

Chaney said government departments are making decisions about ADM use with little consistency or transparency.

“The government wants to find cost savings in the public service and automating decision-making can be a way of achieving those savings,” she said.

“But I think trust in the government is low. There does need to be transparency about when decisions are automated, and when it’s not appropriate for those to be automated, for people to be able to get a clear understanding of why the decision was made and to be really clear about what the pathways are to review that decision.

“This is what people expect of government.”

articles.body:
France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.

The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.

The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.

The attack, which EFS said had occurred overnight on Monday, came as the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in almost a dozen European countries soared as high as 50C (122F), causing millions of euros of food damage.

Retailers in Italy, Germany, Romania and the UK were targeted on Tuesday, after Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems the previous day.

In a wave of attacks in France last month, hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets. A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank said on Wednesday it had been the victim of a cyber-attack.

Something similar may have happened in the US in early August, when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries in at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.

After Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence officials on Tuesday, Thomas Regnier, an EU spokesperson, said the bloc’s agencies were holding urgent discussions with national authorities to formulate a collective response.

“These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said, declining to name any potential culprits. No motive for the attacks is known and no one has claimed responsibility.

A growing range of devices, including commercial refrigeration systems, can be monitored and controlled remotely. Without patching to repair emerging vulnerabilities, internet-connected software can leave code open to hackers.

Some authorities and experts fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks in the aftermath of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Western intelligence officials say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that is taking many forms.

Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos, told the Guardian this week the most plausible attribution scenarios were a “state-based signalling and demonstration of capability” or a lone-wolf hacker.

EFS said it was not directly targeted, with the attacks hitting cold stores run by its contractors. Products stored in the affected rooms, which included plasma bags for transfusions and medicine manufacturing, had been moved to other sites.

It added that France’s national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the health ministry had been alerted, and monitoring of all its equipment had been reinforced.

articles.title: Mattarella: "Urgente una difesa comune europea"
articles.summary: AGI - Procedere con urgenza in direzione di una difesa comune europea. L’appello, reiterato, da parte del Presidente della Repubblica arriva nel giorno in cui si celebrano l’ Unità nazionale e le Forze Armate . Ricorrenza che acquista quest’anno un carico emotivo particolare, per la scomparsa dei quattro militari italiani in Bosnia , ma anche alla luce delle recenti minacce cyber che hanno colpito la cosiddetta “catena del freddo”, in Europa e in Italia. Il messaggio al ministro della Difesa Non sembra un caso, infatti, che il Capo dello Stato sottolinei nel messaggio inviato al ministro della Difesa il fatto che ai “conflitti tradizionali, che continuano a insanguinare ampie aree del mondo, inclusa l’Europa si aggiungono la disinformazione diffusa, la competizione nello spazio, la dimensione cibernetica, l’uso pervasivo dell’intelligenza artificiale e dei sistemi autonomi, domini in cui atti di aggressione risultano oggi in preoccupante e progressiva espansione”. Lo sforzo europeo Concetto ribadito a poche ore dall’incontro di ieri al Quirinale con gli allievi degli Istituti di formazione militare, in occasione della cerimonia di conferimento delle decorazioni all’Ordine militare d’Italia. “In questo contesto è necessario uno sforzo europeo più concreto e più integrato, determinato nel perseguire una interoperabilità degli strumenti militari dei Paesi dell’Unione, in chiave di difesa comune e di rafforzamento dell’Alleanza Atlantica, condizioni imprescindibili per l’equilibrio delle condizioni nel continente”, aveva sottolineato Mattarella. Uno scenario, riprende oggi il Capo dello Stato, “che richiede profonda capacità di rinnovamento, nell’integrare rapidamente le nuove tecnologie e nel garantire capacità concrete per le sfide future”. La Costituzione e la memoria Il tutto nella cornice imprescindibile della Carta Costituzionale, di cui il Presidente della Repubblica è il primo custode: “Il giuramento di fedeltà delle Forze Armate alla Repubblica si nutre dei valori della sua Costituzione”, dice Mattarella, “patrimonio di principi custodito affinché il rapporto con le generazioni che si succedono nella vita del Paese sappia unire la memoria del passato alla speranza per il futuro della comunità, e le atrocità vissute nelle guerre mondiali non abbiano a ripetersi”. Le cerimonie e il cordoglio per i militari in Bosnia Il messaggio di Mattarella precede la cerimonia all’Altare della Patria, prima, e quella a Piazzale Michelangelo, a Firenze, poi. Qui il Presidente della Repubblica ha ritrovato il Generale di Corpo d’Armata e Capo di Stato maggiore della Difesa, Luciano Portolano al quale ha ribadito anche oggi il “profondo cordoglio” e la “grande commozione” per la morte dei quattro militari Italiani nell’incidente in elicottero in Bosnia. “In questa giornata, il deferente omaggio del popolo italiano va a quanti hanno sacrificato la vita per l’Italia, consegnandoci un’eredità di libertà e unità che celebriamo con rinnovata consapevolezza e, oggi, rivolgiamo il nostro pensiero con particolare intensità e cordoglio ai nostri militari che hanno perso la vita nei giorni scorsi in Bosnia-Erzegovina”, le parole di Mattarella. “Celebriamo questa giornata con orgoglio di sempre ma oggi col dolore e col cuore pesante per il lutto che ci ha colpito in Bosnia”, ha esordito Portolano prima di soffermarsi, così come il Capo dello Stato, sulle nuove minacce che impegnano le Forze Armate. Se un secolo fa, ha ricordato il generale di Corpo d’Armata, le linee da difendere avevano un nome, quella del Grappa o quella del Piave, oggi ci troviamo di fronte a nuove e numerose linee da difendere, ha sottolineato. La medaglia d’oro a David Tobini A nome della Repubblica e in onore di tutti i militari caduti nell’adempimento del loro dovere, il Presidente Mattarella ha consegnato la medaglia d’oro al valor militare alla memoria del caporale paracadutista della Brigata Folgore David Tobini, ucciso in uno scontro a fuoco in Afghanistan nel luglio 2011. Il Presidente ha consegnato il riconoscimento alla madre del caduto durante la celebrazione al piazzale Michelangelo. La donna, prima di lasciare il piazzale, ha levato il basco da paracadutista di suo figlio verso il cielo. Lo stesso cielo solcato, poco dopo, dalle Frecce Tricolori che hanno così salutato il Presidente della Repubblica e concluso le celebrazioni.

articles.summary: Dalla scopa gigante blu che lo spazza via al video di lui dietro le sbarre
articles.preview: Donald Trump deriso sui social e 'punito' con la sua stessa arma, vale a dire l'intelligenza artificiale.
